Question: A fifth number, \(n,\) is added to the set of numbers \(\{3, 6, 9, 10\}\) to make the mean of the set of five numbers equal to its median. The number of possible values for \(n\) is
Solution:
The median of five numbers is the third number after they are put in order. Here it depends on where \(n\) falls relative to \(6\) and \(9\). The four original numbers have sum
\[
3+6+9+10=28.
\]
If \(n\le6\), the median is \(6\). For the mean also to be \(6\), the total must be \(5\cdot6=30\), so \(n=30-28=2\). This satisfies \(n\le6\).

If \(6<n<9\), the median is \(n\). For the mean also to be \(n\), the five numbers must total \(5n\). Removing the entry \(n\) leaves the original four numbers with total \(4n\). Thus
\[
4n=28,\qquad n=7,
\]
which lies between \(6\) and \(9\).

If \(n\ge9\), the median is \(9\). The required total is \(5\cdot9=45\), so \(n=45-28=17\). This satisfies \(n\ge9\).

These three cases cover every value of \(n\), with each endpoint included once. Each case gives exactly one valid value, so the possibilities are \(2,7,17\). There are \(\boxed{3}\) values, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
